title: Hydrochlorothiazide: Pressure Down, Electrolytes Down Too
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hydrochlorothiazide lowers blood pressure and promotes sodium/water excretion, but volume depletion, hyponatremia, hypokalemia and metabolic effects can become clinically important—especially in older adults or patients with poor intake, vomiting, renal disease, or interacting drugs.
recognize: Weakness, cramps, confusion, orthostasis, tachycardia or reduced urine output can reflect excessive fluid/electrolyte loss.
Thiazides can worsen hyperuricemia/gout and may alter glucose tolerance.
priorities: Check BP, volume status, sodium/potassium and renal function according to the monitoring plan.
Assess orthostatic symptoms and falls risk after initiation or dose changes.
Escalate severe electrolyte disturbance, syncope, acute kidney injury or acute angle-closure glaucoma symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, sodium, potassium, creatinine, weight/edema, orthostasis, glucose and uric-acid context when clinically relevant.
interventions: Administer earlier in the day when practical to reduce nocturia.
Support prescribed sodium/fluid and potassium plan rather than automatically recommending potassium supplementation.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns about hyponatremia, hypokalemia, volume/electrolyte imbalance and rare acute myopia/secondary angle-closure glaucoma.
Lithium toxicity risk can increase with thiazide diuretics and requires prescriber/pharmacy review.
redFlags: Acute eye pain with vision change
teaching: Rise slowly, monitor BP as instructed, report severe weakness/confusion, and do not self-start potassium or salt substitutes without guidance.
delegationScope: Routine BP/weight collection can be delegated with thresholds; interpretation of electrolyte or renal deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating new confusion in an older adult on a thiazide as dementia before checking sodium and volume status.
oneLinePearl: Thiazides lower pressure by losing salt and water—watch what else gets lost.

title: Tamsulosin: Improve Flow, Prevent the Fall
bottomLine: Tamsulosin relaxes alpha-1 receptors in the prostate/bladder neck to improve BPH symptoms; it does not shrink the prostate and it is not a hypertension drug. Orthostatic symptoms and syncope can create immediate injury risk, especially after starting or restarting therapy.
recognize: Dizziness on standing, weakness or near-syncope may reflect postural hypotension.
Patients planning cataract or glaucoma surgery must tell the eye surgeon about current or past tamsulosin because of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
priorities: Assess baseline BP/orthostasis, urinary symptoms, fall risk and interacting alpha blockers/PDE-5 or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Teach position changes and injury prevention early in therapy.
Escalate syncope, severe hypotension, priapism or worsening urinary retention.
assessMonitor: Trend urinary flow/symptoms, BP/orthostasis, dizziness/falls and surgical eye history.
interventions: Administer approximately after the same meal each day according to labeling and do not crush/open the capsule.
If therapy has been interrupted for several days, clarify the restart plan rather than resuming a higher previous dose automatically.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns about postural hypotension/syncope and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
Tamsulosin should not be combined with other alpha-adrenergic blockers without clinician review.
teaching: Stand slowly and tell the ophthalmologist you take or previously took tamsulosin before cataract or glaucoma surgery.
delegationScope: Routine administration is within medication scope; new syncope/retention requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Stopping tamsulosin only the night before cataract surgery and assuming the surgical risk disappears.
oneLinePearl: Tamsulosin improves flow—but early dizziness can create a fall before urinary symptoms improve.
sourceBasis: DailyMed tamsulosin hydrochloride U.S. prescribing information

title: Finasteride: Shrink the Prostate, Reinterpret PSA
bottomLine: Finasteride blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT and gradually reduces prostate size. Benefits take time, PSA falls substantially during therapy, and crushed/broken tablets pose fetal exposure risk to pregnant people who handle them.
recognize: Symptom relief is slower than with alpha blockers; patients may not notice early improvement.
PSA values are lowered during therapy, so trends must be interpreted with the medication history in mind.
priorities: Confirm the indication and baseline prostate/PSA evaluation plan.
Document finasteride use whenever PSA is reviewed.
Prevent handling of crushed/broken tablets by pregnant people and escalate any exposure concern.
assessMonitor: Trend urinary symptoms, retention/obstructive signs, PSA according to provider plan, sexual adverse effects and breast changes.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce that clinical benefit may take months.
Do not crush tablets for administration without considering reproductive exposure risk and product handling guidance.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling notes PSA is reduced by about 50% after sustained BPH therapy and values must be interpreted accordingly.
Pregnant people should not handle crushed or broken tablets because of potential risk to a male fetus.
complications: Missed prostate-cancer signal if PSA is misinterpreted
redFlags: Confirmed PSA rise from treatment nadir
teaching: Explain the delayed onset, need for continued follow-up and the tablet-handling precaution in pregnancy.
delegationScope: Routine administration can be performed within scope; interpretation of PSA/obstruction changes requires licensed/provider follow-up.
examTrap: Calling a lower PSA 'reassuring' without adjusting interpretation for finasteride therapy.
oneLinePearl: Finasteride shrinks prostate tissue—and the PSA number along with it.
sourceBasis: DailyMed finasteride U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Oxybutynin: Calm the Bladder, Watch Anticholinergic Load
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oxybutynin reduces detrusor overactivity through antimuscarinic effects, but the same mechanism can cause dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention and CNS confusion—especially in older adults with a high anticholinergic burden.
recognize: New agitation, hallucinations, confusion or somnolence may be medication effects rather than a primary psychiatric problem.
Bladder-outlet obstruction, severe GI dysmotility and narrow-angle glaucoma can make anticholinergic therapy unsafe.
priorities: Assess cognition, bowel pattern, post-void/retention symptoms, glaucoma history and total anticholinergic medication burden.
Escalate acute urinary retention, severe confusion, paralytic ileus or acute glaucoma symptoms.
Reassess need/dose if function worsens despite fewer bladder symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend urgency/incontinence, retention, constipation, cognitive status, falls and dry-mouth burden.
interventions: Support bowel/oral-care strategies and hydration according to the patient's overall fluid plan.
Avoid simply adding another anticholinergic for side effects caused by the first.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates use with urinary retention, gastric retention/severe decreased GI motility and uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma.
CNS anticholinergic effects include hallucinations, agitation, confusion and somnolence.
teaching: Report inability to urinate, severe constipation, new confusion or eye pain; avoid overheating because reduced sweating may impair heat tolerance.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; acute retention or delirium requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating new confusion in an older adult with more sedating medication instead of recognizing anticholinergic toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Oxybutynin quiets the bladder by blocking acetylcholine—so watch every other organ that needs acetylcholine too.
sourceBasis: DailyMed oxybutynin chloride U.S. prescribing information

title: Mirabegron: Relax the Bladder, Monitor Pressure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mirabegron activates beta-3 receptors to relax the bladder during filling without the classic anticholinergic burden, but it can raise blood pressure and still cause urinary retention—especially with bladder-outlet obstruction or concurrent antimuscarinic therapy.
recognize: Rising BP after initiation may be drug-related.
New weak stream, suprapubic fullness or inability to void can signal urinary retention even though the medication is used for overactive bladder.
priorities: Check baseline BP, urinary-retention risk and interacting bladder medications.
Monitor BP periodically and assess voiding pattern.
Escalate severe hypertension, acute retention or angioedema.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, urgency/frequency, retention symptoms, renal/hepatic dosing context and adverse effects.
interventions: Swallow extended-release tablets whole and do not crush/divide.
Clarify product/formulation because tablets and extended-release oral suspension are not milligram-for-milligram substitutes.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns mirabegron can increase BP and is not recommended in severe uncontrolled hypertension.
Use caution with bladder-outlet obstruction or concomitant antimuscarinics because urinary retention risk rises.
teaching: Monitor BP as directed and report difficulty urinating, swelling of the lips/tongue, or severe headache/chest symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine administration/BP collection may be delegated with thresholds; acute retention or severe hypertension needs licensed assessment.
examTrap: Choosing mirabegron because it is not anticholinergic and then forgetting to monitor hypertension and retention risk.
oneLinePearl: Mirabegron spares acetylcholine—not blood pressure monitoring.
sourceBasis: DailyMed mirabegron extended-release U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Bethanechol: Make the Bladder Contract Only When the Outlet Is Open
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist used for selected nonobstructive urinary retention. It should not be used when mechanical obstruction is present because contracting the bladder against a blocked outlet can worsen harm; cholinergic effects can also trigger bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, diarrhea and cramping.
recognize: Postoperative/postpartum functional retention or neurogenic bladder atony may respond when obstruction has been excluded.
Wheezing, bradycardia, diaphoresis, abdominal cramping or diarrhea reflect cholinergic effects.
priorities: Confirm that retention is nonobstructive and review asthma, bradycardia/hypotension, peptic ulcer and coronary disease history.
Assess bladder distention, voided volume and post-void response.
Escalate bronchospasm, severe bradycardia/hypotension or worsening painful retention.
assessMonitor: Trend voiding response, bladder distention/residual plan, BP, heart rate, respiratory symptoms and GI adverse effects.
interventions: Administer on the prescribed empty-stomach schedule when ordered to reduce nausea/vomiting.
Maintain fall precautions if dizziness/lightheadedness occurs.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates use with mechanical GI/urinary obstruction, active/latent asthma, pronounced bradycardia/hypotension, peptic ulcer and several other conditions.
Do not use simply because a patient has not voided; identify the cause of retention first.
redFlags: Severe suprapubic pain with inability to void
teaching: Report wheeze, faintness, severe cramps/diarrhea or worsening inability to urinate.
delegationScope: Routine voided-volume collection can be delegated; assessment of retention cause and cholinergic toxicity requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Giving bethanechol to a patient with urinary retention before ruling out an obstructed outlet.
oneLinePearl: Bethanechol squeezes the bladder—make sure there is somewhere for the urine to go.
sourceBasis: DailyMed bethanechol chloride U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Calcium Acetate: Bind Phosphate, Do Not Overshoot Calcium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Calcium acetate binds dietary phosphate in ESRD, so it belongs with meals—but its calcium load can cause clinically important hypercalcemia. Phosphate control is not successful if calcium toxicity, digitalis-sensitive dysrhythmia or vascular calcification risk is ignored.
recognize: Constipation, nausea, anorexia, weakness or confusion can accompany rising calcium.
The medication may reduce absorption of selected oral drugs such as tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones.
priorities: Check calcium/phosphorus trends, meal timing, other calcium/vitamin D products and interacting oral medications.
Administer with meals as prescribed.
Escalate symptomatic or severe hypercalcemia and review digitalis risk when relevant.
assessMonitor: Trend calcium, phosphorus, GI symptoms and medication-timing interactions.
interventions: Avoid unreviewed calcium supplements or calcium-based antacids.
Separate interacting oral medications according to the current product instructions.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates calcium acetate in hypercalcemia and warns that overdose can cause progressive hypercalcemia.
Hypercalcemia can aggravate digitalis toxicity.
teaching: Take with meals and avoid extra calcium products unless the clinician specifically approves them.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; interpretation of calcium/phosphate toxicity requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Giving calcium acetate to a dialysis patient with already elevated calcium because the phosphorus is still high.
oneLinePearl: Calcium acetate binds phosphate by adding calcium—watch both numbers.
sourceBasis: DailyMed calcium acetate U.S. prescribing information, current through 2026

title: Potassium Citrate: Prevent Stones Without Causing Hyperkalemia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Potassium citrate alkalinizes urine and raises urinary citrate for selected recurrent stone disorders, but it also delivers potassium. Renal impairment, heart failure, adrenal insufficiency or other impaired potassium excretion can turn a preventive stone medication into dangerous hyperkalemia.
recognize: Hyperkalemia may be asymptomatic until weakness or ECG changes occur.
Severe vomiting, abdominal pain or GI bleeding can indicate tablet-related GI injury and requires evaluation.
priorities: Review potassium, renal function, stone indication, GI obstruction/ulcer history and interacting potassium-raising medications.
Escalate hyperkalemia, severe abdominal pain/bleeding or new dysrhythmia.
Do not use active urinary infection or major GI transit problems without clinician review because labeling lists important contraindications.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, renal function, urine chemistry/pH according to the stone plan, ECG when indicated and GI tolerance.
interventions: Administer the extended-release product according to meal and swallowing instructions; do not crush without product approval.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling warns potentially fatal hyperkalemia can develop rapidly in patients unable to excrete potassium.
Severe vomiting, abdominal pain or GI bleeding requires discontinuation/evaluation for obstruction or perforation.
teaching: Do not combine with potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless prescribed and keep renal/potassium monitoring appointments.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; hyperkalemia or acute GI symptoms require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Recommending potassium citrate to every kidney-stone patient without checking renal function and potassium risk.
oneLinePearl: Potassium citrate protects against selected stones—but the potassium is real.
sourceBasis: DailyMed potassium citrate extended-release U.S. prescribing information, current 2026

title: Phenazopyridine: Urinary Pain Relief Is Not Infection Treatment
bottomLine: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that can reduce dysuria symptoms but does not eradicate a UTI or treat pyelonephritis. Renal insufficiency increases accumulation/toxicity risk, and the expected orange-red urine can obscure or interfere with color-based urine observations/tests.
recognize: Orange/red urine discoloration is expected and can stain fabric/contact lenses.
Cyanosis, dyspnea, unusual fatigue or low pulse-ox readings with a discordant clinical picture can raise concern for methemoglobinemia, especially with overdose/toxicity.
priorities: Confirm the analgesic role and whether definitive infection evaluation/treatment is also required.
Review renal function before administration.
Escalate cyanosis/methemoglobinemia concern, hemolysis, jaundice or renal/hepatic toxicity.
assessMonitor: Assess dysuria response, renal function context, ongoing infection symptoms and signs of hematologic/oxidative toxicity when indicated.
interventions: Do not allow symptom relief to delay culture/antibiotic follow-up when infection is suspected.
Warn staff/patient that urine color changes can interfere with some urinalysis methods.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling contraindicates phenazopyridine in renal insufficiency.
Methemoglobinemia, hemolytic anemia and renal/hepatic toxicity have been reported, especially with excessive exposure.
redFlags: Persistent fever/flank pain despite symptom masking
teaching: Orange-red urine is expected, but the drug is only for symptom relief; worsening fever, flank pain or systemic symptoms need medical evaluation.
delegationScope: Routine administration can occur within scope; persistent infection or toxicity signs require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Documenting a UTI as treated because dysuria improves after phenazopyridine.
oneLinePearl: Phenazopyridine numbs the symptom—it does not kill the pathogen.
sourceBasis: DailyMed phenazopyridine hydrochloride U.S. prescribing information

title: Fosfomycin: Single-Dose Cystitis Therapy Has a Narrow Job
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Oral fosfomycin tromethamine is a single-dose option for selected uncomplicated acute cystitis in adult women in U.S. labeling. It is not a general-purpose treatment for pyelonephritis, sepsis or every recurrent urinary symptom, so persistent or systemic findings require reassessment rather than repeated self-dosing.
recognize: Lower-tract cystitis symptoms without fever/flank pain differ from pyelonephritis or complicated infection.
Persistent symptoms after therapy may reflect resistance, alternate diagnosis, upper-tract infection or complicated UTI.
priorities: Confirm the prescribed indication and screen for fever, flank pain, pregnancy/complication context, sepsis signs and allergy history.
Prepare the sachet in water; never administer the granules dry.
Escalate persistent/worsening symptoms, systemic illness or suspected pyelonephritis.
assessMonitor: Track symptom response, culture results when obtained, recurrent infection pattern and adverse effects.
interventions: Mix the entire sachet with water according to product instructions and administer promptly.
Reinforce that additional doses should not be improvised for persistent symptoms without clinician direction.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling specifies a single sachet for uncomplicated acute cystitis in women 18 years and older.
The product must be dissolved in water rather than taken dry.
teaching: Complete the prescribed single dose exactly as directed and seek reassessment if symptoms persist or systemic symptoms develop.
delegationScope: Routine administration/teaching reinforcement can occur within scope; assessment for pyelonephritis or sepsis requires licensed clinical judgment and escalation.
examTrap: Using oral fosfomycin as a substitute for urgent evaluation of fever, flank pain and systemic illness.
oneLinePearl: Fosfomycin's single dose is simple—but only for the right lower-UTI patient.
sourceBasis: DailyMed fosfomycin tromethamine U.S. prescribing information, current 2026
